title: Methods, techniques, and asking for consent
introduction: This week Miha's session shifted from making to studying, and from studying to how we treat the people caught up in that study. The first half ran through research methods, techniques and procedures — the scaffolding of a project. The second half was about consent, collaboration and participation, which turned out to be the part I needed to hear most, because it is where ethics stops being abstract and becomes a set of concrete choices.
related_work:
The first principle was the clearest: decide your research question first — what you actually want to know — and only then choose the method. Methods answer 'how'. Ethnography was framed not as a way to prove something right or wrong, but to find out what really happened. Quantitative research deals in numbers, like a star rating; qualitative research needs interpretation and narration, like an open question. And there is a useful split between experiments: a scientific experiment happens in a controlled environment, while an artistic experiment is play — try things, swap materials, and watch what happens. For talking to people, a focus group is sitting together and then analysing the conversation, and interviews come in structured, semi-structured and unstructured forms; the ethics application will ask which one you are using.

The techniques were the doing part: prototyping, testing, observing and feeding back; video and photography as documentation; data visualisation; code experiments; and user-experience testing, which is compulsory for the final project and carries into next semester. The point stressed over and over was to record every stage, because in an academic setting people have to be able to see how you arrived where you did.

Procedures split into two moods. The scientific one is linear: brainstorm and research, then a proposal with an audience and a goal, then development and prototyping, then iterating on feedback, then showing. The creative one is loopier: iterate, and when you get stuck, go backwards, use randomness, think laterally — keep structure so it does not collapse into chaos, but stay flexible within the limits, and let failure be allowed.

The second half was consent, and it grounded everything. Informed consent means a person has all the information before they say yes. Betty Martin's Wheel of Consent describes four ways of giving and receiving — Serve, Take, Allow, Accept — which reframes consent as something with directions rather than a box to tick. Practically, you write out in advance what the equipment is, the stages and the impact, and the participant can withdraw at any time; with collaborators you set roles and timelines in writing, and the record of consent goes into the project. The legal layer is the UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018: processing has to be lawful and transparent, you collect only what is necessary, you do not keep it longer than needed, and you say where it is stored. Sensitive data — race, health, sexual orientation — gets stronger protection, and people have the right to see, correct, delete and withdraw their data. The rule that stuck with me: observing people, taking notes or recording them all have to be announced in advance — no watching in secret.
method: The classroom exercise gave us a reusable skeleton to fill in for any project: list three research methods and how you would use them, the techniques you have used and the ones you plan to, your project procedures, and then the consent half — what data you are collecting, who the participants are, and how you will ask for consent. That last part is where the 'who' gets interesting, because it is not only human participants; the exercise asked us to think about non-human and more-than-human participants too.
results_discussion:
What landed hardest for me was the redefinition of ethnography — not proving a point, but finding out what actually happened. That is a much humbler and more honest position, and it is the one I want to hold in my own research. The split between a scientific and an artistic experiment also clicked: I have been doing the artistic kind all term without naming it — playing with materials and seeing what falls out — and it helps to hear that this is a legitimate method, not a lack of rigour. And 'stay flexible within the limits' feels like a working rule I can actually keep: enough structure not to fall apart, enough room to fail.

The consent section changed how I think about my own projects, especially the dance-and-projection idea I have been circling. That piece will involve another person's body and their performance, which makes consent structural rather than incidental — who owns the image, when can they withdraw, where is the recording kept. The GDPR points are specific and useful rather than vague: collect only what you need, name where it is stored, and remember sensitive data is protected harder. The line about never observing secretly feels obvious when said out loud, but it is exactly the kind of thing that is easy to drift into without realising.
conclusion_future_work: The immediate task is TASK 4, the Artist Statement, due before next week's class on 12 November. Miha described it as writing your position, values and ideas — not just this project, but your whole creative practice — in around three hundred to four hundred words, drawn from the Practice Grid and written as a one- or two-paragraph story of what I actually do. Next week is the Artist Statement crit with written feedback on the Grid, and the week after is how to fill in the university's ERGO ethics approval, which I now understand is not bureaucracy for its own sake but the same consent thinking I learned today, written down.
